explanations.explanation: The song asks, "Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?" She comes up out of the wilderness and she's leaning the whole way. I think that says something good about whoever she's leaning on. My mustache has carried a lot of cookie boxes, but it has never once held up a person.

The Jordan is a real river, but this verse doesn't mention it. The song says she's coming up from the wilderness. Rivers do show up two verses later, when the song says "rivers cannot sweep it away." So keep that river handy, friend, because the song gets to it soon.

The Valley of Elah is a real place. It's where Saul and the men of Israel camped in 1 Samuel 17:2. But this verse doesn't mention it, and the song says she's coming up from the wilderness. Nice try, baker, but that valley belongs to another story.

explanations.answer: Love is as strong as death
explanations.explanation: Right after the request, the song gives its reason: "For love is as strong as death." That's a big comparison, because death is about the strongest thing a person can name. The seal request and the strength of love are tied together in the same breath. That's a lot of weight for one little stamp to carry, and I would know.

The song says the opposite. Its reason is "For love is as strong as death," and it keeps stacking up pictures of love that holds. By verse 7, mighty waters can't quench it. So this song doesn't treat love as something that slips away easily.

A witness is a fine thing to have at a wedding, but the song doesn't bring one up here. The reason it gives is "For love is as strong as death." That's the whole reason, plain and big. No extra people needed in this verse.

The song says the opposite. It calls love's sparks "fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all." A blaze that fierce isn't a flame that quits early. A birthday candle quits early, and trust me, I've met one.

The song calls love's sparks "fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all." That's the biggest fire it can name, and nothing in the verse says it fades. A flame like that doesn't sound like it's running out of steam to me. And the very next verse says water can't put it out.
The song says it flat out: "Mighty waters cannot quench love." You'd think a flood could handle any fire. Not this one. Water is supposed to win that fight, friend, and here it just doesn't.

explanations.answer: They put it out in time
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't give water a win, even a slow one. It says "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." There's no "eventually" in that line. I'm sorry, patient water, but you're not getting in.

The song doesn't give the water even that much. It says "Mighty waters cannot quench love." Not a little, not a bit. If I tried that with a hot tray, I'd be hunting for oven mitts, and the song says love doesn't cool down at all.

The song says that if a man gave "all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned." That's a big pile of wealth, and it still buys nothing. Love isn't something money can purchase. Even a whole house full of treasure can't pay for it, and I got a bargain on a quarter.

The song says his offer "would be utterly scorned." It doesn't say the offer works, and it doesn't say it's even considered. The man gives all the wealth of his house and the offer still gets turned down. Love just isn't for sale in this song.

explanations.answer: What to do for her when she is spoken for
explanations.explanation: The speakers ask, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" They're planning ahead for that day. Somebody in the family is already thinking about the big day. That's the kind of family huddle I know very well.

explanations.answer: How to keep her at home for good
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say anything about keeping her at home for good. The question is what they should do for her on the day she is spoken for. That's a plan for a day that's coming, not a plan to hold her back. Nobody in this verse is locking any doors.

explanations.answer: Who should teach her the old songs
explanations.explanation: Old songs aren't in this verse at all. What the speakers ask is, "What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?" That's the whole question. I'd love a song-teaching committee, but it's not on this agenda.

She says, "So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace." That's how she says he sees her. She starts out talking about being a wall, and she ends up at peace. I think that's a nice place to land, friend.
The song says the opposite. She says she has become in his eyes "like one who brings peace." Trouble doesn't show up anywhere in that line. It's a peaceful verse, so you can put your guard down.

explanations.answer: Like one who is far away
explanations.explanation: Far away isn't what she says. She says she has become in his eyes "like one who brings peace." Nothing in the line puts distance between them. It's all about how he sees her, up close.

She says, "the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon." So Solomon, Israel's king, gets his thousand. Her vineyard is hers to give, and she says what goes where. That's one speaker who knows exactly where her money is going, and I respect that.

The speaker says, "the thousand shekels are for you, O Solomon." So the thousand does go to Solomon, Israel's king. She also says her own vineyard is hers to give. That's a baker with a firm grip on her ledger, friend.

The speaker says, "two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." So the ones who tend the vineyard get paid too. A thousand for Solomon, two hundred for the tenders. I'd like to think those folks went home happy.

The king's officials don't come up in this verse. The speaker says, "two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." Those are the people who work the vineyard. Not a single official gets a shekel here.

This verse doesn't name the daughters of Jerusalem. The speaker says, "two hundred are for those who tend its fruit." So the two hundred go to the ones who work the vineyard. Check the verse next time, friend, because the answer is right there.

The speaker says the opposite: "Let me hear it!" The companions are listening for that voice, and the speaker wants to hear it too. Nobody here is asking for a hush. It's more like a crowd leaning in, and you know I love a crowd.

The speaker says, "You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice. Let me hear it!" So the speaker asks for the voice, not for silence. Everybody's waiting to hear it. If anyone's whispering "shh" in this verse, it isn't the speaker.

explanations.answer: A gazelle or a young stag
explanations.explanation: The last line says, "Come away, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." Both are quick on their feet, and the song ends on that picture of the beloved on the mountains. It's a good last line for a whole song. I'd have tried to fit a cookie in somewhere, and this is better.

Birds don't appear in this last line. The song says to be "like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." Those are animals on the mountains, not in the sky. The dove would've been a sweet pick, though, since I know one dove very well.

The song asks for gentler animals than that. The last line says to be "like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices." No growling in this finish. It ends with a gazelle and a stag, and I think that's a lovely way to close the book.
